title: Default arguments are evaluated once
prompt_md: The single most-reported Python surprise: a default value that is created once, at definition time, and then shared by every call that relies on it. Reason through each case.

questions.stem_md:
```python
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add(1))
print(add(2))
```
What is printed?
questions.explanation_md: The default list is created **once**, when `def` runs, and stored on the function object (`add.__defaults__`). Every call that omits `bucket` mutates that same list, so it accumulates across calls. This is why a function that "remembers" values between unrelated calls almost always has a mutable default.

questions.stem_md:
```python
import time

def stamp(t=time.time()):
    return t
```
A process starts, waits an hour, then calls `stamp()` twice a minute apart. What do the two calls return?

options.md: The same value both times: the time the module was imported, over an hour ago.
Two values a minute apart, each the current time.
The time one hour after import, both times.
`None`, because the default was never re-evaluated.

questions.explanation_md: `time.time()` runs once, while the `def` statement executes at import, not on each call. Both calls return that frozen timestamp. Any default whose value should reflect call time (a timestamp, a fresh id, today's date) must be computed inside the body, with the parameter defaulting to `None`.

sources.locator: Default parameter values are evaluated when the def executes

questions.stem_md: Which of these correctly give each call its own fresh list?

options.md:
```python
def add(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
```

```python
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket = bucket.copy()
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
```

```python
def add(item, *, bucket=None):
    bucket = bucket if bucket is not None else []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
```

```python
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    return bucket + [item]
```

questions.explanation_md: All four avoid mutating the shared default. (a) and (c) are the idiomatic `None`-sentinel form. (b) copies the shared list before touching it. (d) never mutates at all: `bucket + [item]` builds a new list. (a) and (c) are preferred because they signal intent; (b) and (d) work but keep the misleading `[]` in the signature.

questions.stem_md: Which of these default values are a bug risk from sharing? (Select every one that is mutable or freshly computed.)

options.md: `def f(x=0):`
`def f(x=set()):`

questions.explanation_md: Only mutable objects are dangerous, because sharing is harmless if nothing can change the object. `[]`, `{}` and `set()` are mutable; a call that mutates them corrupts the default. Tuples, ints and strings are immutable, so the shared instance can never change: `x=()` is a perfectly safe empty-sequence default, which is exactly why it is idiomatic.

questions.stem_md: You see `field(default_factory=list)` in a dataclass. How does this relate to the mutable-default problem?

options.md: It solves the same problem: a factory is called per instance, so each gets a fresh list rather than sharing one.
It is unrelated; dataclasses do not evaluate defaults at definition time.
It is slower but otherwise identical to `field(default=[])`.
It freezes the list so it cannot be mutated.

questions.explanation_md: `dataclasses` refuses a mutable literal as a `default` precisely because it would be shared across instances (the same bug) and forces you to use `default_factory`, which it calls once per instance. It is the language building the `None`-sentinel discipline into the API so you cannot get it wrong.

hints.md: Anchor on one fact: the expression after `=` in a parameter runs **once**, when the `def` statement executes, not on each call. The resulting object is stored and reused.

So the danger is exactly when that reused object is mutable and the body mutates it. Immutable defaults (`()`, `0`, `""`, `None`) are always safe because the shared instance cannot change. The fix is to default to `None` and build the real value in the body.

Answers: (1) `[1]` then `[1, 2]`: the list is shared. (2) The same import-time value both times. (3) All four fixes are correct. (4) Risky: `[]`, `{}`, `set()`; safe: `()`, `0`, `""`. (5) `default_factory` is the dataclass version of the same fix, one fresh object per instance.
